Questions of this kind have been recently termed ‘reverse’ Littlewood–Offord problems, as the goal is to show a lower bound on the number of signed sum ε1​v1+⋯+εn​vn\varepsilon_{1}v_{1}+\dotsb+\varepsilon_{n}v_{n} that lie in a specified set, rather than an upper bound.




It turns out that Conjecture 1.1 is false as stated, which can be seen in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} by taking an odd number of copies of (1,0)(1,0) and of (0,1)(0,1).
Indeed, this forces all the sums to have norm at least 2\sqrt{2}.
This observation, which is attributed to Erdős, Sárközy, and Szemerédi by Beck [4], was also made by Carnielli and Carolino [6].
Both groups conjectured from this example that Conjecture 1.1 should hold if the radius 11 is replaced with 2\sqrt{2}.
This corrected version of the conjecture of Erdős was proven by Beck [4] in 1983, who moreover obtained the analogous result in every dimension.



Theorem 1.2 (Beck).



For any d≥1d\geq 1, there is a constant cd>0c_{d}>0 depending only on dd such that the following holds.
Let v1,…,vnv_{1},\dotsc,v_{n} be vectors in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with ∥vi∥2≤1\lVert v_{i}\rVert_{2}\leq 1 for each 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n.
If ε1,…,εn\varepsilon_{1},\dotsc,\varepsilon_{n} are independent Rademacher random variables, then




ℙ(∥ε1v1+⋯+εnvn∥2≤d)≥cdnd/2.\displaystyle\Prob\big\lparen\lVert\varepsilon_{1}v_{1}+\cdots+\varepsilon_{n}v_{n}\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{d}\big\rparen\geq\frac{c_{d}}{n^{d/2}}.







Recently, He, Juškevičius, Narayanan, and Spiro [12] rediscovered this result for d=2d=2 with an alternative proof.
While they note that the bound of d\sqrt{d} on the radius of the ball in Theorem 1.2 is optimal, this is not the end of the story for Conjecture 1.1.
Indeed, when d=2d=2, the example that showed that a radius of 2\sqrt{2} is required only works when nn is even.
